Consider the following statements
(i) The sex of a child is determined by what it inherits from the mother.
(ii) The sex of a child is determined by what it inherits from the father.
(iii) The probability of having a male child is more than that of a female child.
(iv) The sex of a child is determined at the time of fertilisation when male and female gametes fuse to form a zygote.
The correct statements are :

options.label: A
options.text: (i) and (iii)

options.label: B
options.text: (ii) and (iv)

options.label: C
options.text: (iii) and (iv)

options.label: D
options.text: (i), (iii) and (iv)

items.answer: A child who inherits an X chromosome from her father will be a girl and one who inherits a Y chromosome from him will be a boy. The sex is therefore decided by the father's contribution at the moment of fertilisation. Thus (b) is the correct option.

items.answer: Gregor Mendel discovered the fundamental laws of inheritance by working on pea plants. He deduced that genes come in pairs and are inherited as distinct units, one from each parent. Mendel tracked the segregation of parental genes and their appearance in the offspring as dominant or recessive traits. He was the first person to figure out genetics well enough to be able to predict the results of the crosses that he made. Some of his findings included the ideas of dominant and recessive factors, independent assortment and segregation of alleles. Thus (a) is the correct option.

items.stem: Which of the following statement for chromosomal theory of inheritance is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Pairing and separation of a pair of the chromosomes would lead to segregation of a factor they carried.

options.label: B
options.text: Behaviour of chromosomes is parallel to the behaviour of genes.

options.label: C
options.text: The two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Chromosomes as well as genes occur in pair.

items.answer: The Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance was consistent with Mendel's laws and was supported by the following observations: (a) during meiosis, homologous chromosome pairs migrate as discrete structures that are independent of other chromosome pairs; (b) the sorting of chromosomes from each homologous pair into pre-gametes appears to be random; (c) each parent synthesizes gametes that contain only half of their chromosomal complement; (d) even though male and female gametes (sperm and egg) differ in size and morphology, they have the same number of chromosomes, suggesting equal genetic contributions from each parent. Thus (a) is the correct option.

items.stem: What is a sex chromosome?
items.answer: A sex chromosome is one which helps in sex determination of an organism. In human males, the sex chromosomes are XY and the gametes (sperms) they produce are of two types: X-bearing and Y-bearing. In females, the sex chromosomes are XX and the gametes (eggs) they produce are of only one type: X-bearing.

items.stem: How do the traits get expressed?
items.answer: DNA is the source of genetic information for making proteins in the cell. The section of functional DNA is called a gene. For example, the height of a plant depends on a hormone. The amount of the hormone depends on the process of its formation. A protein is important for this process. If this protein works efficiently, a lot of hormone will be made. If the gene responsible for that protein has an alteration that makes the protein less efficient, the amount of hormone will be less and the plant will be short. Thus, genes control genetic characteristics or traits of an organism.

items.stem: What are sex chromosomes? What role do they play in determining genetically the sex of an individual in human beings?
items.answer: A sex chromosome is one which helps in the sex determination of an organism. In human males the sex chromosomes are XY and the gametes (sperms) they produce are of two types, X-bearing and Y-bearing. items.stem: How do proteins control the characteristics that are inherited? Explain with the help of an example.
items.answer: (a) A segment of functional DNA (a gene) is the information source for making proteins. (b) Proteins which are enzymatic in nature control a metabolic pathway which in turn regulates a specific characteristic. For example, the gene for plant height codes for an enzyme of the hormone (growth) pathway: an efficient enzyme makes enough hormone and the plant is tall, while a defective enzyme makes less hormone and the plant is short. Thus any defect in the DNA (gene) alters the nature of the protein and so changes the expressed character.

items.stem: How do Mendel's experiments show that traits may be dominant or recessive?
items.answer: When Mendel cross-bred plants of two different traits of a character — a tall pea plant (TT) and a dwarf pea plant (tt) — all the plants of the F₁ generation were tall. Thus only the dominant trait was visible in this generation. But when the plants of the F₁ generation were self-crossed, the two traits got separated in the plants of the F₂ generation: not all the F₂ plants were tall, and one-fourth of them were short. The appearance of the tall character in both the F₁ and F₂ generations shows that it is the dominant character, while the absence of the dwarf character in the F₁ generation and its reappearance in the F₂ generation shows that dwarfness is the recessive character.

items.stem: With the help of two suitable examples explain why certain experiences and traits earned by people during their lifetime are not passed on to their next generations. When can such traits be passed on?
items.answer: Learning skills such as swimming or dancing, earned by people during their lifetime, are not passed on to the next generation. If a person knows swimming or dancing it is not necessary that this trait is seen in the progeny, because learning a new skill does not change the genes of the germ cells. Such acquired traits occur in the somatic (body) cells only and do not involve the germ cells or their genetic material, so they cannot be transmitted. Such a trait can be passed on only if the change affects the DNA of the germ cells (gametes), because only the germ-cell DNA is handed on to the offspring.

items.stem: How did Mendel's experiments show that different traits are inherited independently? Explain.
items.answer: When a cross was made between a tall pea plant with round seeds and a short pea plant with wrinkled seeds, the F₁ progeny plants were all tall with round seeds, which indicates that tallness and round seeds are the dominant traits. When the F₁ plants were self-pollinated, the F₂ progeny consisted of some tall plants with round seeds and some short plants with wrinkled seeds — the parental combinations — as well as new combinations such as tall plants with wrinkled seeds and dwarf plants with round seeds. The appearance of these new combinations shows that the tall/short traits and the round/wrinkled seed traits are inherited independently of each other.

items.stem: How did Mendel explain that it is possible that a trait is inherited but not expressed in an organism?
items.answer: Yes, it is possible. In Mendel's experiment, when pure tall pea plants were crossed with pure dwarf pea plants, only tall pea plants were obtained in the F₁ generation. On selfing the pea plants of the F₁ generation, both tall and dwarf pea plants were obtained in the F₂ generation. The reappearance of the dwarf pea plants in the F₂ generation proves that the dwarf trait was inherited but not expressed in the F₁ generation. A recessive trait does not express itself in the presence of the dominant trait. So it is possible that one trait may be inherited but may not be expressed in an organism.

items.stem: Explain Mendel's experiment with peas on inheritance of characters considering only one visible contrasting character.
items.answer: Mendel drew his conclusions on the inheritance of characters considering only one visible contrasting character, i.e. a monohybrid cross, with garden peas. (i) He studied homozygous (pure) plants of tall (TT) and short (tt) varieties. (ii) He crossed them and obtained the F₁ progeny. (iii) He found that in the F₁ progeny all the plants were tall. (iv) He selfed the plants of the F₁ progeny, which were hybrid (Tt). items.stem: (a) What is the role of autosomes? (b) Why is it that an offspring receives traits from both the parents?
items.answer: (a) Autosomes are the chromosomes which contain the genes for all somatic traits. They are identical in males and females and they have no role in the determination of sex. (b) During sexual reproduction two haploid gametes, one from the father and one from the mother, each having half the number of chromosomes, fuse to form the diploid zygote. The zygote therefore carries chromosomes from both the parents, bearing different genes for different traits, so the offspring receives traits from both parents.

items.stem: In one of his experiments with pea plants, Mendel observed that when a pure tall pea plant is crossed with a pure dwarf pea plant, in the first generation (F₁) only tall plants appear. (a) What happens to the traits of the dwarf plants in this case? (b) When the F₁ generation plants were self-fertilised, he observed that in the plants of the second generation (F₂) both tall plants and dwarf plants were present. Why did it happen? Explain briefly.
items.answer: (a) The dwarf trait of the plants is not expressed in the presence of the dominant tall trait. (b) In the F₂ generation both the tall and dwarf traits are present in the ratio 3 : 1. This shows that the traits for tallness and dwarfness were both present in the F₁ generation, but dwarfness, being the recessive trait, does not express itself in the presence of tallness, the dominant trait. During gamete formation the genes for both characters separate independently and do not affect each other's function or inheritance, so the dwarf trait reappears in the F₂ generation.

items.answer: In humans, genetically the sex of a child is determined by the father and not by the mother because in the father there are two types of sex chromosomes present, X and Y, whereas in the mother both sex chromosomes are X. items.stem:
Mendel worked out the rules of heredity by working on garden pea using a number of visible contrasting characters. He conducted several experiments by making a cross with one or two pairs of contrasting characters of pea plant. On the basis of his observations he gave some interpretations which helped to study the mechanism of inheritance.
(i) When Mendel crossed pea plants with pure tall and pure short characteristics to produce F₁ progeny, which two observations were made by him in F₁ plants?
(ii) Write one difference between dominant and recessive trait.
(iii) In a cross with two pairs of contrasting characters
RRYY (Round Yellow) × rryy (Wrinkled Green)
Mendel observed 4 types of combinations in F₂ generation. By which method did he obtain F₂ generation? Write the ratio of the parental combinations obtained and what conclusions were drawn from this experiment.
(iv) Justify the statement “It is possible that a trait is inherited but may not be expressed”.
items.answer:
(i) Observations made by Mendel in the F₁ progeny of the monohybrid cross: the F₁ generation consisted of only tall plants, which means that only one of the parental traits was seen, and not some mixture of the two. (ii) Differences between dominant and recessive traits are as follows:
Dominant traitRecessive trait
The trait which appears in the F1 progeny is dominant.The trait which remains hidden or which not appear in the F1 progeny is the recessive trait.
2It appears in more numbers.It appears in less number.
(iii) (1) Mendel took two pure breeding plants, one having round and yellow seeds (RRYY) and the other having wrinkled and green seeds (rryy). (2) The parents were cross pollinated and the F₁ generation was raised, in which all the plants produced had round and yellow seeds. (3) The F₂ generation was obtained by selfing (self-pollinating) the F₁ plants, and in it he found four combinations of phenotypes as given below. Dihybrid phenotypic ratio ⇒ 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, i.e. the two parental combinations (round yellow and wrinkled green) appear as 9 and 1, while the two new combinations (round green and wrinkled yellow) appear as 3 and 3. Dihybrid genotypic ratio ⇒ RRYY – 1, RrYY – 2, rrYY – 1, RRYy – 2, RrYy – 4, rrYy – 2, RRyy – 1, Rryy – 2, rryy – 1. Conclusions drawn from the dihybrid cross (Law of Independent Assortment): (a) any pair of unit factors or genes controlling different characters can segregate or separate independently of all other unit factors during the formation of gametes; (b) for one pair, whichever unit factor is received, it does not influence the outcome of segregation of any other pair. (iv) Yes, it is possible that a trait is inherited but may not be expressed. For example, when pure tall pea plants are crossed with pure dwarf pea plants, only tall pea plants are obtained in the F₁ generation; but when the members of the F₁ generation are selfed, the dwarf trait which had disappeared in the F₁ generation reappears in the F₂ generation. Hence we can say that it is possible for a trait to be inherited but not expressed.

items.stem: In a pea plant, the trait of flowers bearing purple colour (PP) is dominant over white colour (pp). Explain the inheritance pattern of F₁ and F₂ generations with the help of a cross following the rules of inheritance of traits. State the visible characters of F₁ and F₂ progenies.
items.answer:
As the trait of flowers bearing purple colour (PP) is dominant over white colour (pp), the monohybrid cross between the two pea plants can be represented as: PP (purple) × pp (white) → F₁ all Pp. On self-pollination of the F₁ plants, the F₂ genotypes are PP : Pp : pp = 1 : 2 : 1.
(a) In the F₁ generation all the pea plants have purple flowers, because purple is dominant and Pp expresses purple.
(b) In the F₂ generation the pea plants with purple flowers and white flowers are in the ratio 3 : 1, the white flowered plants being the homozygous recessive (pp).

items.stem: "The sex of a new born child is a matter of chance and none of the parents may be considered responsible for it." Justify this statement with the help of a flow chart showing sex-determination in human beings.
items.answer:
The sex of a newborn depends on what happens at the time of fertilization. (i) If a sperm of the male carrying an X chromosome fertilizes the ovum of the female carrying an X chromosome, then a girl child will be born and the child will have the XX combination of sex chromosomes. (ii) If a sperm carrying a Y chromosome fertilizes the ovum carrying an X chromosome, then the child born will be a boy with the XY combination of sex chromosomes.
Flow chart: Father (XY) × Mother (XX) → gametes X and Y from the father, only X from the mother → X sperm + X egg = XX (girl) or Y sperm + X egg = XY (boy), in equal probability.
Since the mother contributes only X chromosomes and it is entirely a matter of chance whether an X-bearing or a Y-bearing sperm reaches the egg first, the sex of the newborn is a matter of chance and none of the parents may be considered responsible for it.

items.stem: (a) What are dominant and recessive traits? (b) "Is it possible that a trait is inherited but may not be expressed in the next generation?" Give a suitable example to justify this statement.
items.answer:
(a) The trait which can express its effect over a contrasting trait is called the dominant trait, whereas the trait which cannot express its effect over the contrasting trait, or which gets suppressed by the contrasting trait, is called the recessive trait. Thus an inherited trait which is not expressed will be a recessive trait.
(b) Yes. In Mendel's experiment, when pure tall pea plants were crossed with pure dwarf pea plants, only tall pea plants were obtained in the F₁ generation. On selfing the pea plants of the F₁ generation, both tall and dwarf pea plants were obtained in the F₂ generation. The reappearance of the dwarf pea plants in the F₂ generation proves that the dwarf trait was inherited but not expressed in the F₁ generation. The recessive trait does not express itself in the presence of the dominant trait. So it is possible that a trait may be inherited but may not be expressed in an organism.

items.stem: How do Mendel's experiments show that (i) traits may be dominant or recessive? (ii) the inheritance of two traits is independent of each other?
items.answer:
(i) Traits may be dominant or recessive. When Mendel cross-bred plants of two different traits of a character — a tall pea plant (TT) and a dwarf pea plant (tt) — all the plants of the F₁ generation were tall, so only the dominant trait was visible in this generation. But when the plants of the F₁ generation were self-crossed, the two traits got separated in the plants of the F₂ generation: not all the F₂ plants were tall, and one-fourth of them were short. The appearance of the tall character in both the F₁ and F₂ generations shows that it is a dominant character, whereas the absence of the dwarf character in the F₁ generation and its reappearance in the F₂ generation shows that dwarfness is the recessive character.
(ii) When a cross was made between a tall pea plant with round seeds and a short pea plant with wrinkled seeds, the F₁ progeny plants were all tall with round seeds, which indicates that tallness and round seeds are the dominant traits. When the F₁ plants were self-pollinated, the F₂ progeny consisted of some tall plants with round seeds and some short plants with wrinkled seeds — the parental traits — as well as new combinations such as tall plants with wrinkled seeds and dwarf plants with round seeds. Thus it may be concluded that the tall/short traits and the round/wrinkled seed traits are inherited independently.

items.stem: Define genetics. What is the contribution of Mendel in this branch of biology?
items.answer:
Genetics is the study of the inheritance of genetic characteristics from the generation of parents to the offspring, and of the laws relating to such transmission or inheritance. In other words, genetics is the "science of heredity and variation".
Mendel's contribution: Mendel observed the occurrence of contrasting characters in various generations of the garden pea (Pisum sativum). On the basis of his observations, Mendel interpreted that these contrasting characters (e.g. tall and dwarf plants, wrinkled and smooth seeds) are controlled by "factors". He considered each and every character as a unit which is controlled by a "factor". What Mendel called "factors" — the carriers of hereditary information — are now known as genes.

Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage.

A gene is the basic physical and functional unit of heredity. Genes are made up of DNA. Most of the characters or traits of an organism are controlled by the genes. Genes are actually segments of DNA guiding the formation of proteins by the cellular organelles. These proteins may be enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and structural components of different types of tissues. In other words, DNA/genes are responsible for the structure and functions of a living body. The genotype of an individual controls its phenotype.

Gene T → responsible for synthesis of efficient enzyme (protein) → more production of growth hormone → result in tall plants
Gene t → responsible for synthesis of less efficient enzyme → less production of growth hormone → result in short plants

(i) Two pea plants, one with round green seeds (RRyy) and another with wrinkled yellow (rrYY) seeds, produce F₁ progeny that have round, yellow (RrYy) seeds. When F₁ plants are selfed, the F₂ progeny will have a new combination of characters. Choose the new combination from the following.
I. Wrinkled, green  II. Wrinkled, yellow  III. Round, green  IV. Round, yellow
(a) I and II  (b) I and IV  (c) II and III  (d) I and III

(ii) A section of DNA providing information for one protein is called
(a) Gene  (b) Nucleus  (c) Chromosomes  (d) Trait

(iii) Which one of the following is present in the nucleus?

items.answer:
(i) (b) I and IV. The parental combinations are round-green and wrinkled-yellow, so in the F₂ generation the newly appearing (recombinant) types are wrinkled-green (I) and round-yellow (IV).
(ii) (a) Gene. A gene is the segment of DNA that carries the information for the synthesis of one protein.
(iii) (d) All of these. The nucleus contains chromosomes, which are made of DNA, and the genes are the functional segments of that DNA.
